title: Looking back: the thought

cards: At the end of a long course, a student is handed a blank card and one instruction: in a single sentence, what did you learn? It can be harder than the exam.
For a long block this year, the path put four big questions to the Granth. What is God like? Who am I, really?
How should I live? What is this world? A few days ago the path ran back through it at speed.
Today, slowly: one line for each question, then the blank card comes to you.

teach.h: GOD: BEYOND QUALITIES, AND WITH THEM.
teach.b: God first. In the Sukhmani, Guru Arjan holds two things together. In paraphrase: He Himself is beyond all qualities, and He is with qualities too.
Beyond every form, and present in every form. The hymns keep both halves, which is why the Granth can call God formless on one page and Beloved, Friend and Husband on the next.
Then the self. In the Asa di Var, a salok of Guru Angad names the trouble plainly. In paraphrase: ego is a long, deep illness, and the medicine is found within it too.
Haumai, the I that keeps grabbing the center, isn't the whole of a person. The same self that grabs can learn to let go. Then how to live.
Elsewhere in the Asa di Var, Guru Nanak puts a whole ethic in one line.

In paraphrase: sweetness and humility, Nanak, are the essence of every virtue and every good. Not a long list of rules: two plain qualities, kept in the voice and in the way a person stands among others. And the world.

teach.h: WORLD: AIR THE GURU, EARTH THE MOTHER.
teach.b: The Japji's final salok says, in paraphrase: air is the Guru, water the father, and the great earth the mother. The world isn't a waiting room. It's family, and it teaches.
Four lines, one shape. It all arrives as poetry, much of it sung, and that matters. Sikh thought isn't a form to sign.
It's a set of lines to carry, and to keep turning over.

how: Sikhs learn the Gurus' thought by hearing and singing the Granth's hymns and through katha, the spoken explanation of a hymn, often returning to lines like the Mool Mantar and the close of the Japji.

o: a list of beliefs every Sikh has to sign up to
a year-end look at four big questions in Sikh thought
a test of how many hymns you can say from memory

games.q: four questions, four lines: tap the pairs.
p: air the Guru, earth the mother

s: in the Japji's closing salok, the world is only a waiting room
it calls air the Guru, water the father, and the great earth the mother.
Guru Nanak names sweetness and humility as the essence of virtue
in the Asa di Var: sweetness and humility are the essence of every virtue and every good.
the Gurus call God only formless
Guru Arjan writes that God is beyond qualities and with qualities too.

games.q: a salok of Guru Angad names ego a long, deep illness. where does he say the medicine is?
o: within the same place as the illness.
games.why: in the Asa di Var: ego is a deep illness, and the medicine is found within it too.

practice: Suppose a friend asked you tonight, over tea, what the Gurus teach: not what the books say, but what you would say.

Let the four lines go by slowly, beyond qualities and with them, ego and its medicine, sweetness and humility, air the Guru and earth the mother, then wait for your own sentence, a few plain words for where you stand today.
If nothing comes, that's an answer too; if you pray, bring the question itself into the prayer.

wordCard.voice: Looking back. Today, at Sikh thought: God, the self, how to live and the world, each held in a line of the Granth. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: nirgun, beyond qualities; the Sukhmani says God is nirgun and sargun, with qualities, too.

carryVoice: Your line: what I think now. Where you stand today is worth knowing. That's today, done.
